newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq sends first group of travellers to Syria.
newsitem.headline: Iraq sends first group of travellers to Syria.

text.p: A first group of Iraqi travellers left for Syria on Tuesday in the first such visit since ties between Baghdad and Damascus were severed in 1980, travel agencies in Baghdad said.
Iraq and Syria, which are ruled by rival factions of the Baath party, decided last month to reopen their borders after a closure of nearly 17 years.

"Some 60 people aboard two buses travelled today to Damascus via the 850 km (510 miles) long Iraqi-Syrian highway for the first time (since 1980)," Majed Hussein, owner of a travel agency in Baghdad, told Reuters.
He said 23 travellers out of the group were Iraqis while the rest were Syrians and Lebanese living in Iraq. They went to Damascus either for tourism or to visit relatives, he added.
Hussein said another trip was organised for Thursday and he expected more Iraqis to join in. He said he would open a branch of his agency in Damascus to bring Syrians to Iraq.

Syria's relations with Baghdad deteriorated in 1980 when Damascus sided with Iran in the 1980-88 Iraq-Iran war and further worsened with Syrian troops joining the U.S.-led Western alliance forces that drove Iraqi troops out of Kuwait in 1991.
But signs of economic and diplomatic rapprochement have emerged over the past two months between the two neighbouring countries.
Iraqi and Syrian officials have pledged to resume trade links between the two Arab states. Syria wants to sell Iraqi goods under its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

Under the deal, which went into effect in December, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy urgent needs for Iraqis hard-hit by U.N. sanctions imposed for Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Iraq's Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh said on Sunday while opening a Syrian medical exhibition in Baghdad that his ministry signed $20 million worth of food contracts with Syria under the oil pact.

Baghdad has asked the U.N. sanctions committee to allow it to use a Syrian-Iraqi border point to handle some of its purchases under the deal. Food, medicine and other humanitarian goods purchased by Baghdad under the oil deal are now reaching the country through Umm Qasr port in southern Iraq, Jordan and Turkey.
The U.N. sent earlier this month a group of experts to examine the Iraqi-Syrian outlet but no results have yet been announced.
